The Week the Election Pushed Back

Courts rejected a last-ditch campaign to challenge ballots and voters, then Democrats took back Congress

```markdown This was the week of the midterm elections, and it unfolded as a test of whether an administration losing public support could use the machinery of federal law enforcement to shape the outcome anyway. Over seven days, the Justice Department pressed an aggressive legal campaign against ballots, election workers, and voting-rights lawyers, only to watch courts at every level strike it down. Then voters went to the polls and delivered a verdict of their own.

The pattern was set before the week properly began. On Saturday, a federal judge in California issued a restraining order stopping the Justice Department from threatening or coercing election workers into segregating ballots cast by suspected noncitizens, describing the department's conduct as intimidation. That same weekend, a federal judge dismissed Trump's defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal with prejudice, ruling he had failed to show actual malice in its reporting on an alleged Epstein-related letter — a reminder that press-freedom protections remained intact even as other fronts heated up. Meanwhile, the U.S. Attorney for Alaska announced a sweeping criminal investigation into election officials and the voting-rights lawyer Marc Elias, acknowledging openly that it was unclear whether any crime had occurred. Away from the courts, fear of immigration enforcement led several cities to cancel or scale back Día de los Muertos celebrations, and in Mississippi, a police department tied to a contested fatal shooting was hit by arson.

By Monday, the judicial rebuke became a cascade. Federal judges in multiple jurisdictions rejected Justice Department demands to segregate or invalidate ballots in California, along with challenges to state election procedures elsewhere. The Supreme Court separately declined to intervene on the administration's side, issuing no dissents. A Ninth Circuit panel briefly granted a stay on a Voting Rights Act question, but it was swiftly set for en banc review. Taken together, it amounted to a near-unanimous judicial rejection of federal attempts to override state election administration in the days before a vote.

The pressure on election defenders intensified rather than easing. The Justice Department sent target letters to Marc Elias and other Democratic lawyers in the Alaska investigation and charged six lawful permanent residents in California with voter fraud — moves critics described as unusually aggressive given their timing. Trump then publicly branded Elias a criminal on social media following the department's defeat, and at a rally in Iowa he repeatedly called Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist," including a remark about installing a metal detector in Congress for him. It was rhetoric from a sitting president aimed at once at a political opponent's faith and at a private attorney representing his adversaries' interests.

Other threads ran alongside the ballot fights. Democrats, anticipating a shift in congressional control, signaled plans to use budget leverage and oversight authority to constrain the administration's Iran policy. The Justice Department deployed roughly 1,000 monitors to polling places in all 50 states and did not rule out sending immigration agents as well — a presence that raised concerns about voter intimidation even though no major disruptions were ultimately reported. A former FBI official in Chicago, Douglas DePodesta, filed suit alleging he had been pressured to investigate Trump's opponents and then forced out, implicating FBI Director Kash Patel and senior Justice Department leadership. And Harmeet Dhillon, who had redirected the department's Civil Rights Division away from traditional enforcement and toward targeting universities, resigned — the first senior departure in what would become a larger post-election exodus.

On Tuesday, the central legal battle reached its conclusion. The Supreme Court issued its final rejection of the Justice Department's effort to force California to set aside roughly 20,000 ballots, again with no dissents recorded, closing out the week's most consequential ballot-access fight. Elsewhere, a federal judge ruled that Iowa's years-long denial of a Satanic Temple holiday event at the state capitol was unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination and ordered the state to approve it within a week. A man previously pardoned for threatening Nancy Pelosi after January 6 was arrested for posting threats to execute federal judges who had presided over Capitol attack cases — a reminder that the aftershocks of that day had not fully settled. And on the eve of the election, Trump held a press conference at the Lincoln Memorial focused largely on a reflecting-pool renovation, claiming he had kept "every single promise," even as he signed proclamations declaring an Anti-Communism Week and asserting an American claim to the development and settlement of outer space.

Wednesday was election day, and the results were unambiguous. Democrats retook both the House and the Senate. Incoming committee leaders Robert Garcia and Ron Wyden signaled plans for aggressive investigations into the administration, including Elon Musk's role in government efficiency efforts, the Trump family's business dealings, abuses by immigration enforcement, and the Epstein matter. It was the restoration of a congressional check that had been largely absent for two years, with subpoena power explicitly invoked.

The president's response did not take the shape of acknowledgment. He claimed on social media that he would have won "in a landslide" had his own name been on the ballot, then the next day held a twenty-minute press event centered on his White House ballroom renovation rather than the election results. He posted repeated criticisms of Fox News, faulting its polling and ratings for the outcome. And in a move that stood apart from the rest of the week's domestic drama, he announced on election night that $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel would end at year's end — explicitly tying the decision to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed's use of that aid figure in his campaign messaging. It was a foreign policy shift presented, in the president's own words, as a reaction to domestic political criticism. Elsewhere that day, federal prosecutors dropped all charges against Kseniia Petrova, a Harvard researcher who had been detained for months over frog embryo samples, after allegations the case had been retaliatory, and Colorado voters rejected a ballot measure that would have expanded police cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Thursday brought another judicial check, this time aimed at the president's personal legacy project. Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a fourteen-day restraining order blocking construction of a 250-foot triumphal arch at Memorial Circle, ruling that the project likely violated the Commemorative Works Act's requirement for congressional authorization — a reversal of approval granted just a day earlier by a planning commission aligned with the administration. In California, outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom commuted all 548 death sentences in the state to life without parole, the largest clearing of a death row in modern American history, in one of his final acts before leaving office. Dhillon's resignation from the Civil Rights Division became official amid a broader reckoning: the department had lost 27 of 28 lawsuits seeking state voter-file access, including defeats before numerous judges the administration itself had appointed. Trump, meanwhile, signed a proclamation designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments, a move explicitly intended to prevent future administrations from altering his interior design choices. Elsewhere, billionaire Leon Black sued Congressman Robert Garcia for defamation over statements tying him to Jeffrey Epstein's crimes, after Black had declined to comply with a House oversight subpoena, and the first lady hosted a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire ceremony at the White House while the president met separately and privately with a Russian negotiator.

The week closed on Friday with the balance of power visibly shifting. Incoming Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, now commanding 54 to 56 seats, pledged that Democrats would block any "crappy" nominees to the Supreme Court, the lower courts, and the cabinet. A federal judge formally entered the restraining order halting the triumphal arch's construction. Trump announced that Susie Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, would be replaced by immigration hardliner Stephen Miller — continuing a pattern of departures among senior women in the administration. More Justice Department officials resigned, including John Eisenberg and Jason Reding Quiñones, whose departure effectively ended a politically charged investigation into alleged conspiracy among former officials to violate Trump's rights. Trump's attorneys also appeared before a New York appellate panel to argue that his 34-count felony conviction from the hush-money case should be overturned, raising both the underlying legal theory and claims of presidential immunity. And in Mississippi, a Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith remained separated by fewer than 2,000 votes, with national legal teams and the NAACP deploying monitors over roughly 20,000 uncounted ballots ahead of a looming certification deadline.

Taken as a whole, the week offered a rare, compressed demonstration of how American institutions are supposed to function under strain. A federal law enforcement apparatus attempted, in the days before an election, to intimidate workers, invalidate ballots, and investigate the lawyers defending the vote — and courts, including a Supreme Court that issued no recorded dissents, said no, repeatedly and specifically. Voters then delivered their own judgment, handing control of Congress to the opposition in numbers large enough to leave little room for dispute. What followed was not an acknowledgment of that verdict but a retreat into symbolism and personnel change: proclamations, a ballroom tour, a monument to interior design choices, and a reshuffling of the president's inner circle toward a more combative posture. What the week leaves behind is a documented record — court rulings, a 27-to-1 litigation count, and an election tally — that any future account of this period will have to reckon with, whatever interpretation it ultimately offers. ```
